title: The reason in things
hookLine: Stoics saw a reason running through all things

cards: Cut an apple across the middle, not top to bottom, and you'll find a five-pointed star. A sunflower's seeds curl out in two sets of spirals, one clockwise, one counter.
Your heartbeat speeds up on the stairs and settles when you sit. The tide comes in about twice a day, a little later each day. None of it looks random.
There's an order to things, and the Stoics gave that order a name: logos.

teach.b: Logos is a very busy Greek word: word, speech, story, account, reason, even ratio. It comes from a verb meaning to say, and before that, to gather or pick out. You hear it in logic, or biology, the account of life.

Long before Zeno, a philosopher named Heraclitus of Ephesus used logos for the order behind the world, and complained that it's common to all of us, yet most people live as if they had a private understanding of their own.
For them, the logos is the reason running through everything, the rational pattern that shapes a seed into a tree and keeps the stars in their tracks.
They pictured it as active and alive, a kind of fiery breath moving through matter, and gave it many names at once: nature, fate, providence, even Zeus or God.
Stoics disagreed among themselves about details, and the sources are fragmentary, so it's fair to say we only see the outline. Here's why it matters for a person, not just the cosmos.

teach.h: A SMALL SHARE IN EACH OF US.
teach.b: Each of us, they said, carries a small share of that same reason. When you think clearly, you're doing on a small scale what the world does on a large one.
That's why living by reason and living by nature were the same thing to them.
The same Greek word appears in the Gospel of John, where Christians read it their own way; for the Stoics, the logos was the pattern itself.

how: Many who practice Stoicism today treat the logos as the rational order of nature, whether they understand it religiously or not, and try to think clearly as their share in it.

games.q: Heraclitus says the logos is common to all. what does he complain most people do?
o: live as if they had a private understanding.
games.why: Heraclitus complains that though the logos is shared, most live as if their understanding were private.

practice: Start with the nearest pattern: your breath. In, a turn at the top, out, a pause at the bottom; nobody is running it, and it runs. If your mind wanders, that's a pattern too: come back, one turn, then the next.

wordCard.voice: Logos. Greek for word, reason or account: for the Stoics, the reason running through all things, shared in each of us.

carryVoice: Your line: the pattern. A seed, a star, a clear thought: one reason running through them all. That's day two hundred eighty-nine.
